# Developing an artificial intelligence literacy framework: Evaluation of a literacy course for senior secondary students using a project-based 

# learning approach 

## Siu-Cheung Kong [a,b,\*, Man-Yin William Cheung](#computers-and-education-artificial-intelligence) [c, Olson Tsang](#computers-and-education-artificial-intelligence) [b ](#computers-and-education-artificial-intelligence)

c _Talent and Education Development Office, City University of Hong Kong, China_ 

ARTICLE INFO ABSTRACT 

_Keywords:_ The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) in the workplace is pressuring employees to learn how to harness this Artificial intelligence literacy technology. The goal of promoting AI literacy is to equip educated citizens with the readiness to apply AI. The Ethics aim of this study is to provide evidence to guide the development of an AI Literacy Framework to prepare Framework 

educated citizens to participate in future society. We report on a 14-h AI literacy course for senior secondary 

Problem-solving Project-based learning students, emphasising problem-solving competence development and adopting the project-based learning 

approach. One hundred and twenty-eight students completed the course, and a mixed-methods analysis was conducted to evaluate the results. A post-course test showed that the course had improved the students’ ability to use AI concepts in solving real-life problems. Self-surveys indicated that the students showed a significant improvement in their metacognitive strategies in problem-solving, and had a better understanding of the ethical boundaries and principles that govern the use of AI for problem-solving. A thematic analysis of data drawn from focus group interviews with the students and their self-reflective writings indicated that PBL supported them in reflecting critically on the ethical use of AI and developing their problem-solving competence. Future studies should consider validating the course evaluation instruments among a more extensive and diverse population.

2\. **Background of Study** 

_2.1._ _The four dimensions of AI literacy_ 

As discussed in the “Introduction” section, AI literacy is essential to enable educated citizens to harness AI and use it to contribute to society. The elements of AI literacy can be grouped into four dimensions. At the most fundamental level, educated citizens must have an adequate con- ceptual understanding of AI (Touretzky et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2023; Wong et al., 2020). Across nearly all the proposals of what constitutes AI literacy, knowledge and concepts of AI are consistently identified as a crucial component. One of the earliest AI literacy frameworks (AILFs) was developed by Long and Magerko (2020), who stressed the impor- tance of knowing what AI algorithms can do and how they can be applied. The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development \[OECD\] (2021) deemed an understanding of AI concepts as central to educated citizens’ ability to evaluate and engage with AI. More recently, Ng et al. (2022) noted that AI concepts without any prerequisite knowledge comprise the most fundamental level of AI literacy, enabling educated citizens to comprehend the principles of AI rather than simply using its applications. Additionally, many AILFs place a strong emphasis on conceptual understanding of AI, as opposed to generating novel AI algorithms. 

The cognitive dimension of AI literacy relates to the understanding of AI concepts, including the underlying logic of AI algorithms such as supervised learning (e.g. linear regression and the K-nearest neighbour algorithm), unsupervised learning (such as K-means clustering), and neural networks, and how these algorithms can be adapted as solutions to real-life problems ([Chiu et al., 2022;](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing) Marques et al., 2020; Ng et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023). Conceptual understanding is the foundation on which educated citizens apply AI in everyday life, evaluate their perceptions of and feelings about AI, and advance their AI knowledge and competence. The focus of conceptual understanding is on the knowledge and skills needed to use and apply AI models, which are AI algorithm-based mathematical models trained on vast amounts of data to perform specific tasks; students do not need to comprehend complex mathematical formulae or write programming code to apply such models. Teaching AI concepts also lowers the barriers of entry to AI literacy ([Kong, Cheung, & Zhang, 2022;](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing) Long & Magerko, 2020) and enables its promotion to as many educated citizens as possible, pre- paring them for the AI revolution ([Chaka, 2023)](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing). There is a need to improve educated citizens’ ability to leverage publicly available AI tools and generate solutions to problems they encounter at work or in their daily lives. The goal is to allow educated citizens to partner and collaborate with AI, becoming active participants in the AI world instead of mere passive consumers. Indeed, recent studies have increasingly focused on the teaching of AI to non-computer science or non-mathematics experts who nonetheless regularly engage with AI ([Laupichler et al., 2023)](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing). Our previous research ([Kong et al., 2021,](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing) [2022a)](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing) confirmed that in both university and senior secondary student populations, programming is not a prerequisite for the acquisition of AI concepts. However, students do require a knowledge of basic mathe- matical concepts, such as mean, standard deviation, slope, and Euclidean distance, to grasp the rationale of AI algorithms. The conceptual understanding of AI also encompasses the strengths and limitations of algorithms, along with the types of problems for which they may be applicable and suitable (Ng et al., 2023; Pintrich, 2002). Educated citizens need this knowledge to readily apply AI to augment their skillsets, advance their productivity and creativity, and solve real-life problems. AI concepts are also valuable, if not indis- pensable, in evaluating AI-based solutions formulated by oneself or others, which is a key step in problem-solving using AI. 

Concepts alone are not enough to fully harness AI; educated citizens also need to solve diverse problems that go beyond conceptual under- standing (Ng et al., 2023) and involve metacognitive processes. Thus, the capacity to apply AI tools for problem-solving makes up the 

metacognitive dimension of AI literacy. Adapting the model proposed by Schraw et al. (2006), problem-solving using AI can be summarised as consisting of the following four stages: (1) defining the problem; (2) identifying relevant AI concepts and solutions; (3) selecting, planning, and executing the AI-based solutions; and (4) evaluating the results of the solutions. 

When solving problems with AI, educated citizens need to be acutely aware of the AI concepts they are familiar with, retrieve those concepts, and then consider and select the concepts relevant to their specific problems (Torrey, 2012). These concepts range from the capabilities and weaknesses of algorithms to the way these algorithms can be imple- mented as solutions. Notably, citizens must know how to collect and process suitable data (Whang et al., 2023), and must understand how to select an existing AI algorithm or model suitable for the problem. After executing the selected model as an AI-based solution, educated citizens need to interpret and evaluate the results. If the solution leads to un- expected outcomes, the AI problem-solving process must be repeated to either modify the current solution or devise a novel solution (Schraw et al., 2006). Importantly, improving the solution requires educated citizens to be conscious of the limitations of their understanding of AI concepts. By further strengthening their conceptual understanding, educated citizens can formulate novel strategies and self-enhance their problem-solving competence, which is a core feature of metacognition (Winne & Azevedo, 2014). 

Often overlooked but of equal importance to AI concepts and AI problem-solving skills is educated citizens’ psychological readiness to interact with AI, which forms the affective dimension of AI literacy. Psychological readiness is required for educated citizens to proactively use AI as a tool to solve real-life problems, and to fully harness AI technology to contribute to their professions and to society ([Chiu et al., 2022;](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing) [Dai et al., 2020)](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing). As a central element of readiness, _empowerment_ increases educated citizens’ confidence in applying AI for problem-solving ([Kong et al., 2021)](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing). Empowerment can be subclassified into four components, two of which are especially critical to problem-solving with AI. In the context of problem-solving, ‘AI self-- efficacy’ refers to educated citizens’ confidence in successfully har- nessing AI to solve real-life problems ([Bandura, 1982)](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing). AI self-efficacy is closely related to educated citizens’ sense of capability, as the feeling of being able to solve problems with AI increases their self-efficacy ([Chai et al., 2021)](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing). Another empowerment factor key to AI problem-solving is educated citizens’ creative self-efficacy, which is the self-belief in their creativity (Tierney & Farmer, 2011). As described above, the formula- tion of novel ideas is a major feature of the problem-solving process, particularly when a previous solution has failed. Thus, the ability to produce new AI-based solutions, which frequently require creative or divergent thinking, is integral to successful AI problem-solving. Multiple studies have shown a reciprocal positive association between creative self-efficacy and creativity (Puente-Díaz & Cavazos-Arroyo, 2017; Tierney & Farmer, 2011). Notably, Royston and Reiter-Palmon (2019) reported the pivotal role of creative self-efficacy in mediating students’ creativity and their creative thinking in problem-solving. The remaining two factors of empowerment – meaningfulness and impact – motivate educated citizens to interact with and harness AI. In the AI context, ‘meaningfulness’ refers to educated citizens’ perception of the personal significance of using AI for problem-solving (Thomas & Velthouse, 1990), while ‘impact’ refers to their view of how problem-solving with AI can affect society ([Frymier et al., 1996)](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing). Educated citizens need to realise the value and power of applying AI to their everyday lives if they are to be internally motivated to use AI to solve challenges (Lin et al., 2021). It has been proposed that student-centred, self-directed course designs, such as project-based learning (PBL), are conducive to empowering learners ([Hains & Smith, 2012)](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing). Self-directed projects allow students to select personally mean- ingful problems and experience how AI can be used to solve them. A personal and active learning experience empowers learners to use AI for problem-solving, conferring upon them a sense of capability and 

achievement, and helping them recognise the importance of solving problems with AI ([Dede & Barab, 2009)](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing). 

The last dimension of AI literacy, the social dimension, relates to how educated citizens can contribute to society by using AI to solve problems (Long & Magerko, 2020; Ng et al., 2023; Touretzky et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2023). AI usage inevitably has both favourable and adverse im- pacts, and educated citizens must appropriately balance these effects. When applying AI to problem-solving, they must consider the ethical concerns associated with AI-based solutions and their implementation ([Chiu et al., 2022;](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing) [Kong et al., 2023;](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing) Wang et al., 2023; Wong et al., 2020). They also need to decide whether AI is truly needed to solve a specific problem (Sturm et al., 2021). Recent AI ethical guidelines have emphasised various ethical principles ([European Commission, 2022;](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing) White House Office of Science and Technology Policy \[OSTP\], 2022; United Nations Educational Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO, 2022), the three most important of which are fairness, beneficence, and human autonomy ([Kong et al., 2023)](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing). Collectively, these principles dictate that the benefits and risks of AI-based solutions must be distributed evenly, with the former outweighing the latter, and human users should ultimately be accountable for the effects of AI-based solutions. These AI ethical principles, which have recently received intense scholarly attention ([Jobin et al., 2019;](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing) [Kaur et al., 2023;](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing) Vinuesa et al., 2020), may be regarded as constraints within which educated citizens solve real-life problems with AI ([Floridi et al., 2020)](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing). Fig. 1 shows the four dimensions of our proposed AILF and its main content. The four dimensions are cognitive, metacognitive, affective, and social. 

_2.2._ _Project-based learning in AI education programmes_ 

PBL is a pedagogical approach in which students create a product (Prince & Felder, 2007). PBL has characteristics typical of situated learning, including collaboration, real-world contexts, and self-reflection ([Herrington & Oliver, 2000)](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing). In practice, Ng et al. (2023) discovered that more than 60% of AI education programmes adopted a collaborative PBL design. PBL begins with a driving problem to be solved ([Krajcik & Shin, 2014)](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing), around which learners set goals ([Kokotsaki et al., 2016)](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing) and approach the problem creatively and critically from multiple perspectives ([Karan & Brown, 2022)](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing). PBL also allows learners to apply theoretical ideas in a hands-on manner, transforming concepts into concrete solutions (Tomlin et al., 2019) and, in the process, becoming more confident and empowered (Tsybulsky & Muchnik-Rozanov, 2019). PBL therefore also corresponds to the ultimate stage of the revised Bloom’s taxonomy, namely, to create ([Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001)](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing). Students who create their own AI-based solutions to a self-identified problem will, in the process, develop their ability to use AI to solve 

**Fig. 1.**

problems as well as their confidence in using AI in real-life scenarios. Compared with traditional instruction, PBL results in better awareness of the value of the subject, self-perceived competence, self-efficacy, and career aspirations ([Beier et al., 2018)](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing). 

_2.3._ _The research gap_ 

The four dimensions of AI literacy discussed above are collectively 

required for educated citizens to harness AI and contribute to society. There is, to the best of our knowledge, no comprehensive framework of AI literacy in the literature. While previous studies have proposed several AILFs, they each emphasise a different set of core components of AI literacy. For example, early AILFs (Long & Magerko, 2020; Touretzky et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2020) focused on the cognitive and social di- mensions, highlighting AI concepts and the ethical use of AI. The AILFs developed in other studies ([Chiu et al., 2022;](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing) [Dai et al., 2020;](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing) Zhang et al., 2023) included citizens’ confidence in engaging and readiness to engage with AI and their perception of the relevance of AI, recognising the affective dimension as an integral constituent of AI literacy. How- ever, few AILFs emphasise the use of AI for problem-solving, the meta- cognitive dimension in our AILF. The AILF developed by Ng et al. (2022) is one of the few to recognise that AI literacy involves the application of AI concepts to solve problems in real-life situations. 

We propose a comprehensive four-dimensional AILF for senior sec-

ondary students. We applied a mixed-methods analysis to answer the following research questions: (1) Can PBL help senior secondary stu- dents develop their conceptual understanding of AI? (2) How can senior secondary students’ ability to solve problems using AI be developed? (3) Can senior secondary students be empowered to use AI to solve prob- lems? (4) Can senior secondary students develop ethical concepts and understand the relevant ethical principles when solving problems with AI? 

3\. **Methodology** 

_3.1._ _Course participants_ 

This study is part of an AI literacy project in a university in Hong 

Kong, following a donation in support of a programme that publicly recruited students from all secondary schools in Hong Kong to develop their AI literacy. The AI literacy course reported in this study is the third part of the AI literacy programme. The first two parts were two 9-h courses on AI concepts in machine learning and deep learning ([Kong, Cheung, & Tsang, 2022)](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing), totalling 18 h. Those two courses also covered the five steps of machine learning, which serve as a guideline for 

Four dimensions of the AI literacy framework: Cognitive, metacognitive, affective, and social. 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

problem-solving using AI. The five steps are (1) problem definition; (2) data collection; (3) data pre-processing; (4) model training; and (5) inference and prediction. Participation was entirely voluntary, and participants could opt out at any time during the programme. We ob- tained informed consent from all participants of this study. Ethical approval to collect data in this study was granted by the Human Research Ethics Committee of the university (Ref. No. A2020-2021-0204 and 2021-2022-0325). 

One hundred and twenty-eight senior secondary students completed the first two courses, and then proceeded to the third course, which is reported here. Regarding data collection for this study, all 128 students completed the AI conceptual test and the four surveys administered during the study. Additionally, 97 students contributed self-reflective essays, and 12 students joined focus group interviews. Over half of the students reported a lack of a programming background, as the course did not require any knowledge of programming. The demographics of the students are detailed in Table 1. 

_3.2._ _Course administration and design_ 

The whole programme was non-credit-bearing and free of charge. The students were openly recruited from all secondary schools in Hong Kong. They received a certificate of completion after completing each course. The instructors of the course were all well qualified academi- cally, having either a doctoral degree, master’s degree, or postgraduate diploma in education. 

The entire course consisted of workshops that lasted for a total of 14 

1. It adopted a PBL pedagogical approach. Ethical principles and con- siderations around the usage of AI, with a focus on the beneficence of AI, fairness of AI, and human autonomy, were first introduced to the par- ticipants, who then conducted an AI problem-solving project in groups. They first brainstormed a problem that could be solved with AI-enabled tools, and the instructors then demonstrated the use of AI-enabled tools such as Google Teachable Machine (for image, sound, and posture recognition), Microsoft Azure QnA Maker (for chatbot generation), and Microsoft Azure Machine Learning Studio (for quantitative data analysis and prediction). As these tools were either freely available or institu- tionally subscribed to, the participants could readily access and use them. The instructors then organised project consultations for individual groups. The five steps of machine learning were reiterated and emphasised, as the participants were asked to follow these steps as a guideline when designing the AI-based solutions. An example of an AI- based solution that the participants developed was an AI squatting coach, which discerned whether users’ squatting posture was correct. The instructors indicated that the most frequently used mode of Google Teachable Machine, the image recognition mode, may not be optimal, and suggested the posture mode instead. They also offered suggestions on how to collect postural data, such as through the online dataset portal Kaggle or by taking pictures. Furthermore, the instructors guided the participants in considering the ethical implications of their AI-based solutions and how those concerns could be mitigated. The participants then engaged in approximately 6 h of collaborative project work in which they produced AI-based solutions to their self-defined problems. They collected data and trained their AI models to generate a solution, in the process reflecting on the challenges, potential enhancements, and 

**Table 1** Distribution of students by year of study and programming background. Gender 

ethical considerations pertaining to their AI-based solutions. Next, during project presentation, the students demonstrated these solutions, discussed the associated ethical issues and considerations, reflected on the challenges encountered throughout the problem-solving project, and proposed potential enhancements to the solutions. The students were expected to discuss ethical implications not limited solely to the final solution product but also related to data collection, data processing, and other stages of the overall AI problem-solving project. Table 2 shows how the course design was aligned with the four dimensions of AI literacy. 

_3.3._ _Instruments_ 

Both quantitative and qualitative instruments were used for course evaluation. The quantitative instruments were as follows: (1) an ‘AI Concepts for Problem-solving’test consisting of seven questions to assess the participants’ ability to use AI concepts to solve real-life problems; (2) a ‘Metacognitive Strategies for Problem-solving in PBL’ survey with four items to measure how the collaborative project affected the participants’ metacognition when solving problems with AI; (3) an ‘Empowerment in Using AI for Problem-solving survey’ with 17 items to measure the participants’ degree of empowerment in using AI for problem-solving; 

4. an ‘AI Ethics’ survey with 12 items to assess the participants’ un- derstanding of AI ethical principles and issues ([Kong, Cheung, & Tsang, 2022)](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing); [Kong, Cheung, & Zhang, 2022n](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing)d (5) a ‘Literacy in Using AI for Problem-solving’ survey with 12 items to evaluate the participants’ perceptions of their competence in using AI for problem-solving. The qualitative instruments were as follows: (1) focus group interviews that included an in-depth discussion of the participants’ learning from the course; and (2) a self-reflective essay on AI in English or Chinese. The instruments were developed based on the four dimensions of AI literacy. The ‘AI Concepts for Problem-solving’test was designed to measure the capability of the students in applying the machine learning and deep learning concepts that they had acquired in the 18-h founda- tion course to real-life scenarios. An excerpt from the ‘AI Concepts for Problem-solving’test can be found in [Appendix 1.](#statements-on-open-data-and-ethics) The ‘Metacognitive Strategies for Problem-solving in PBL’ survey was designed to measure

The ‘Empowerment in Using AI for Problem-solving survey’ was designed to study the students’ empowerment and psychological readiness to apply AI technology for problem-solving and contains items on the four factors of empowerment defined in the ‘Background of Study’ section, namely impact, creative self-efficacy, AI self-efficacy, and meaningfulness. These four compo- nents were covered by four, four, five, and four items, respectively. An excerpt from the AI Empowerment for Problem-solving survey can be found in [Appendix 2.](#statements-on-open-data-and-ethics) The ‘AI Ethics’ survey was used to evaluate the students’ understanding of ethical principles when solving problems with AI. It comprised questions on the three major AI ethical principles described in the ‘Background of Study’ section, namely human auton- omy, beneficence of AI, and fairness of AI. Each of the principles was covered by four items. An excerpt from the ‘AI Ethics’ survey can be found in [Appendix 3.](#statements-on-open-data-and-ethics) The ‘Literacy in Using AI for Problem-solving’ survey was designed to assess the students’ overall self-perception of their ability to solve problems with AI. All items of the Literacy in Using AI for Problem-solving’ survey can be found in Table 8. 

All items of the surveys consisted of single statements designed to measure the attitudes of the participants. Each statement was answered by selecting responses from an evenly spaced Likert scale, ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree) to measure the participants’ level of agreement/disagreement with the target statement (Likert, 1932). Table 3 shows the results of normality and reliability tests for the five quantitative instruments. The Kolmogorov–Smirnov test was used to test for normality of the data, and it showed the score distributions of all five instruments significantly deviated from a normal distribution (see Table 3), justifying the use of non-parametric statistical analyses. The reliability of the instruments was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha, a measure of consistency, i.e. the degree to which the items in an instru- ment measure the same feature. The greater the value of Cronbach’s alpha, the more consistent the items in an instrument, and the more reliable that instrument (Tavako & Dennick, 2011). All but one survey had a Cronbach’s alpha over 0.95, which the literature has suggested to be an ideal value (Tavako & Dennick, 2011). 

The focus group interviews were guided by five questions covering the cognitive, metacognitive, affective, and social aspects of AI literacy. The students were asked about the specific AI concepts they had learnt from the course and how the course had prepared them to apply AI in their daily lives and in their future endeavours of study or work. They 

**Table 3** Results of tests of reliability (Cronbach’s alpha) and normality (Kolmogor- ov–Smirnov test) of the **‘AI Concepts for Problem-solving’ test**, **‘Meta-** **cognitive Strategies for Problem-solving in PBL’ survey**, **‘Empowerment in Using AI for Problem-solving survey’**, **‘AI Ethics’ survey**, and **‘Literacy in Using AI for Problem-solving’ survey**, based on the post-course results of the instruments. 

were also interviewed on the influence of the problem-solving project on their feelings towards learning about and using AI. Lastly, the students were asked for their views on the impact of AI on future society. An excerpt from the focus group interview questions, which were semi- structured, can be found in [Appendix 4.](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing) The self-reflective essay in- strument, in which the students wrote about AI in English or Chinese, was designed to be less structured. There was no specific topic or guiding question, and the students were free to express their views, including what they knew about AI, how they may harness AI, and how AI may affect society. 

As the qualitative component of our mixed-methods analysis, we conducted thematic analysis, which is widely used to analyse qualitative data ([Braun & Clarke, 2006)](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing). Data from both qualitative instruments were used, namely the transcripts of the focus group interview with 12 of the participants and the post-course self-reflective essays written by 97 participants. The use of multiple data sources for thematic analysis is recommended, as it allows for a better-supported, more robust conclu- sion than single-source thematic analysis ([Creswell & Poth, 2017;](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing) Peel, 2020; Xu & Zammit, 2020), and it has been adopted in recent studies ([Araújo et al., 2017;](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing) [El-Jardali et al., 2014;](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing) Stott et al., 2018). The analysis was performed following the procedure described in [Braun and Clarke (2006),](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing) pursuant to which we (1) read through the interview transcripts and reflective essays to familiarise ourselves with the data; 

2. generated initial open codes; (3) identified the patterns and cat- egorised the codes into axial codes; (4) developed the themes; and (5) established the relationships between the themes. More specifically, we selected words and phrases that were frequently repeated in the tran- scripts and reflective essays to derive the initial open codes. These open codes were then classified into axial codes based on their underlying meanings. Lastly, the axial codes were grouped into high-level themes and were named such that they captured the meanings of all corre- sponding codes. We also derived relationships between the themes and codes from the source materials.

4. **Results and discussion** 

This section reports the changes in the participants’ ability to apply AI concepts for problem-solving, their metacognitive strategies when solving problems with AI under the PBL approach, their empowerment in using AI for problem-solving, their understanding of ethics when using AI for problem-solving, and their literacy in using AI for problem- solving.

The thematic analysis provided further support for the use of PBL pedagogy to develop senior secondary students’ skills in using AI to solve problems. It also reinforced the quantitative finding that problem- solving projects are an effective way to empower senior secondary stu- dents and nurture their confidence in applying AI to future challenges. Specifically, the projects offered the students opportunities to apply AI concepts in a hands-on manner and personally observe the process and output of using AI to solve real-life problems. However, ‘empowerment to use AI’ was the theme with the fewest coded instances, making up only 16.38% of the total. Cultural factors may influence the way stu- dents express their confidence and engage in learning activities. In Asian, especially Confucian, cultures, humility and modesty are highly valued, and overt displays of confidence are sometimes viewed as inappropriate or boastful ([Leung & Cohen, 2011;](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing) Markus & Kitayama, 1991). This cultural norm may influence how the students’ discussed empowerment in interviews and self-reflective essays (Lu et al., 2022). 

5. **Conclusion, implications, limitations, and future studies** 

This study evaluated an AI literacy course designed to endow senior secondary students with the knowledge and skills to solve real-life problems using AI. The course adopted a PBL pedagogical approach in which students, guided by instructors, developed AI applications to solve self-defined problems. Both the quantitative and qualitative results indicated that the students’ competence in using AI to solve problems had increased, as had their confidence and readiness to do so. As the students already possessed conceptual knowledge of machine learning and deep learning, our course’s PBL approach offered them the opportunity to put these concepts into practice (Tomlin et al., 2019). The results of the ‘AI Concepts for Problem-solving’ test implied that PBL had improved the students’ understanding of the AI concepts that they had to review when formulating an AI-based solution in the problem-solving project. The ‘Metacognitive Strategies for Problem-solving in PBL’ survey and ‘Literacy in Using AI for Problem-- solving’ survey also indicated that PBL had helped the students build their problem-solving competence. After the course, the senior second- ary students were not only capable of solving diverse problems but also better able to engage in processes requiring metacognitive strategies, such as self-improving their problem-solving skills, evaluating and 

formulating novel solutions, and recalling and applying relevant AI knowledge. These results suggest that PBL is a suitable pedagogical approach to fostering students’ conceptual understanding of AI and to further developing their competence in using AI for problem-solving. Our AI literacy course also empowered the senior secondary students to apply AI to solve real-life problems. The significant improvement in their AI self-efficacy and creative self-efficacy components showed that after the course, the students had increased confidence in their ability to use and creativity in using AI for problem-solving and were readier to do so than they were before the course. This result is consistent with recent studies that have evaluated PBL-based AI courses ([Bühler et al., 2022;](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing) Williams et al., 2023; Xia et al., 2022; Zhan et al., 2022). PBL allowed the students to apply AI concepts in a hands-on manner, promoting their interest in applying AI to solve problems, not merely knowing about the technology. Successful completion of the project also conferred upon the students a sense of capability in harnessing AI to solve problems. PBL’s enhancement of the students’ creative self-efficacy is a notable finding, as improving and devising alternative AI-based solutions requires cre- ative thinking and self-belief in creativity. The ceiling effect may explain the nonsignificant enhancement of the participants’ perceptions of the impact and meaningfulness of problem-solving with AI ([Lee et al., 2021)](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing). Before the course, the students already had a noticeable aware- ness of the power and value of using AI for problem-solving. In a previous study ([Kong, Cheung, & Tsang, 2022)](#ai-self-efficacy-creswell-j-w--poth-c-n-2017-qualitative-inquiry-and-research-design-choosing), we argued that senior secondary students required increased guidance and time to develop their comprehension of abstract AI ethical principles, as this proved more challenging to them than to university students. Thus, the instructors in the present AI literacy course modified their teaching methods accordingly. This revised pedagogical approach significantly improved the participating senior secondary students’ understanding of ethical principles and their consideration of ethical issues. This enhanced ethical awareness and comprehension, which enables the participating students to understand the constraints within which they can apply AI, is crucial for AI-based problem solving. 

In summary, this study has two important implications, one theo- retical and the other practical. First, this study provided an initial sub- stantiated theoretical framework for guiding the design of AI literacy programmes. This study provided groundwork and justification for a comprehensive four-dimensional AILF, comprising cognitive (concep- tual understanding of AI), metacognitive (the ability to solve problems with AI), affective (psychological readiness to apply AI for problem- solving), and social (ethical considerations of AI-based solutions) di- mensions. This framework may serve as a guide for the design of future AI literacy education programmes. The framework acknowledges that personally meaningful experiences are essential for the development of students’ AI literacy, such as through student-centred problem-solving projects. This is corroborated by the findings of this study, in which the AI problem-solving project enabled students to apply the AI concepts they had acquired, realise their ability to use AI, understand the benefits of AI application in real-world scenarios, and reflect on the ethical im- plications of the AI-based solutions they had developed. Second, this study provided empirical evidence that PBL is a viable teaching approach for developing the AI literacy of senior secondary students. PBL was shown to strengthen senior secondary students’ understanding of AI concepts, develop their confidence, and psychologically empower them to apply AI for solving problems they encounter in study, work, or their daily lives. The study also confirmed that senior secondary students require more guidance to fully understand the ethical principles and issues surrounding AI. 

The study also has two limitations. First, there is a need to broaden the database of participants. Having a greater number of students study the AI literacy course would enable us to further substantiate the results obtained in this study. Additionally, the geographical homogeneity of the participants may have affected the generalisability of the results. As such, future research could benefit from including students across different geographical regions, thereby ensuring broader applicability of 

the findings. The second limitation concerns instrument validation, which was potentially limited in scope in this study. To ensure the reliability and validity of the instruments, future studies should consider validating them among a more extensive and diverse population. This would help confirm the effectiveness of the instruments across a wider context and populace, thereby enhancing the robustness of our research conclusions. 

As discussed in the “Introduction” section, with the increasing role of AI in society, educated citizens need to be literate in AI to harness this technology and work synergistically with it. By partnering with AI and being augmented by this partnership, educated citizens can apply AI to solve real-life problems and contribute to society. We verified that our AI literacy course equipped senior secondary students with a knowledge of essential AI concepts, developed their AI problem-solving competence and ethical understanding, and empowered them to apply AI to solve real-life problems. Students with such skills are prepared for an AI future, being able to proactively harness AI and shape society’s future response to the AI revolution. Future studies should investigate whether and how our AI literacy course can prepare educated citizens to participate in determining and shaping the direction in which society will move in the AI age. 

## Statements on open data and ethics 

The data that support the findings of this study have not been made available. The surveys and tests are variously available in full in Tables 5 and 8 or as excerpts in the appendices. Ethical approval for this study was granted by the Human Research Ethics Committee of the authors’ university (Ref. No. A2020-2021-0204 and 2021-2022-0325). Partici- pation in this study was entirely voluntary, and the participants could opt out at any time during the study. Informed consent was obtained from all participants.
